text.content: Give the chart a clear title and labels so readers can interpret the intended comparison. text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
In Excel for the web, select A1:B3 and use Insert > Charts to choose a suitable type. Give the chart a clear title such as “Order amount by branch” and labels that make the comparison interpretable. The title is an example, not a required naming pattern.

Right-click the chart and choose Select Data. In Data > Setup, assign A2:A3 to Horizontal Axis > Horizontal Field and add B2:B3 under Vertical Axis > Add Field, checking that the category and value fields occupy the intended axes. Inspect the source range and plotted series in the chart task pane, correcting names or ranges as needed. Then use Format to check the chart title, axis titles, and displayed data labels.

The useful output is a chart whose type and field placement answer the business question. Selecting a range and accepting a first appearance is not the same as checking that the chart uses the intended categories and values.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A chart type should fit the question, not merely look attractive. Bars support category comparisons and lines support trends over time. Also inspect the plotted source and field placement; a clear title cannot fix a chart using the wrong range.

text.content: Suppose an operations manager asks, “Which branch has the largest total order amount in this extract?” Clarify that the desired analysis is a branch-level total, not average order amount or a count of orders.

text.title: Ad Hoc Business Reporting
text.content: Start by clarifying the business outcome or question the analysis should address.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: A spreadsheet pivot table can summarize source data with fields placed in Rows, Columns, and Values. Present the answer prominently and include enough supporting detail for the audience to understand it. Select a table or range, insert a PivotTable, place grouping fields in Rows and the metric in Values, and select an aggregation that answers the business question.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical source, North amounts are 40 and 60 and South amount is 30. Select the source table or range and insert a PivotTable. Place Branch in Rows and Amount in Values, then select the aggregation that answers the question: a total for this request. The resulting totals are North 100 and South 30. Columns can also structure the summary when the business question needs another grouping dimension, but this simple question does not require one.

Present the answer prominently: “North has the larger total in this extract: 100 compared with South’s 30.” Include enough supporting detail for the audience to understand what was summarized and which source the answer refers to. The stated result is for the hypothetical extract, not a claim about all business activity.

The useful output is a targeted answer supported by a relevant summary. Starting with a business question helps you choose grouping and aggregation; opening a spreadsheet does not itself define what the analysis should accomplish.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A count, average, and total answer different business questions. Do not accept a Values summary without checking the aggregation needed. Also, the report should state the answer clearly rather than make the reader infer it from a PivotTable alone.

practice_anchor.objective: Produce a one-page spreadsheet analysis answering the operations manager's question: which branch has the largest total order amount in the supplied extract? Use Branch and Amount source columns containing North amounts of 40 and 60 and a South amount of 30. State the clarified question, create a PivotTable with Branch in Rows and Amount in Values, and check that the aggregation is Sum.
practice_anchor.success: The one-page analysis prominently states that North has the largest total in this extract: 100 compared with South's 30. A supporting PivotTable shows those branch totals using Sum of Amount, and the report identifies the supplied hypothetical extract as its source without extending the conclusion beyond it.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible the Branch and Amount source records, the PivotTable field placement with Branch in Rows and Amount in Values using Sum, the resulting North 100 and South 30 totals, and a prominent answer scoped to the supplied extract.

segments.label: Summarize sales with PivotTable grouping fields and summed amounts
segments.summary: Create a PivotTable by selecting the source data and using Insert PivotTable. Converting the source range into a named table first helps accommodate future data updates. The PivotTable field areas organize the summary: placing Salesperson in Rows and Amount in Values produces sales totals by salesperson. Excel chooses a sum or count depending on the field; in this example, the numeric Amount field defaults to Sum. Currency formatting and banded rows make the figures easier to read. Adding Geography beneath Salesperson in Rows creates a two-level grouping; moving Geography into Columns provides a matrix layout. Alternatively, placing Geography in Filters restricts the salesperson totals to a selected geography, such as New Zealand.

bridge_note.before: Watch how grouping fields and Amount turn source sales records into targeted summaries. Notice the default aggregation, then check that it matches the business question rather than accepting it automatically.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates PivotTable construction and grouping. It does not teach initial stakeholder-question clarification or a prominent audience-facing answer; the text covers both and reinforces choosing the appropriate aggregation.

required_facts.statement: Sprint Planning collaboratively establishes the work for the iteration.
Review important backlog items collaboratively and select work that can be completed within the iteration.
Inspect candidate items for clear descriptions and sufficient detail, and refine uncertain items before selection.
Selection considers the Developers’ capacity and past performance rather than an externally imposed commitment.

text.content: Imagine the team is planning an iteration containing instruction-access work. Sprint Planning collaboratively establishes the iteration’s work, rather than receiving a commitment imposed from outside the Developers.

text.title: Sprint Planning (BA Involvement)
text.content: Sprint Planning collaboratively establishes the work for the iteration.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Review important backlog items collaboratively and select work that can be completed within the iteration. Inspect candidate items for clear descriptions and sufficient detail, and refine uncertain items before selection. Selection considers the Developers’ capacity and past performance rather than an externally imposed commitment.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Review important backlog items together. For this hypothetical case, the instruction-display item has clear behavior and acceptance detail, while an amendment item still leaves the intended result unclear. Inspect candidate descriptions and refine uncertain items before selection. Select work that can be completed within the iteration.

Consider Developers' capacity and past performance in selection. A stakeholder’s strong preference does not replace that consideration. The BA can help clarify requirements and questions, while the planning discussion remains collaborative rather than becoming a BA-issued delivery promise.

The useful contribution is transparent candidate work with enough detail for the team to reason about selection. If an item cannot yet be understood, record and resolve the uncertainty instead of silently assuming its scope. The example does not prescribe how many items belong in the iteration; that decision depends on the collaborative assessment and Developers' capacity and past performance, not on a universal quota for business analysis work.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: High priority does not by itself establish that all requested work fits. Selection considers Developers' capacity and past performance. Clarifying a requirement also does not authorize the BA or another external participant to impose the Developers' commitment.

practice_anchor.objective: Review a candidate sprint backlog containing instruction-display and amendment items. Flag items whose descriptions or acceptance detail leave the intended result unclear, and record the clarification needed before selection.
practice_anchor.success: The unclear amendment item is flagged with its unresolved intended result identified. The instruction-display item is recognized as sufficiently clear for selection consideration, without treating clarity alone as proof that it fits the Developers’ capacity.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the candidate instruction-display and amendment items side by side, with their descriptions, acceptance detail, unresolved questions, and clarification flags. Make the amendment item’s unclear intended result visible, and distinguish clarity for selection consideration from a commitment to deliver.

notes: Respect developer selection considerations; no prescribed sprint item counts.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and effective backlog management.
The Product Owner may delegate backlog-management work but remains accountable for it.
Developers are responsible for sizing the work and deciding how selected work is performed.
Clarify backlog items collaboratively while respecting the Product Owner’s ordering accountability and the Developers’ delivery decisions.
source_refs: scrum_guide#https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html — Product Owner; Product Backlog; Sprint Planning

text.content: Suppose the BA is helping clarify an instruction-access item while the Product Owner and Developers discuss delivery. Product Owner accountability includes maximizing product value and effective backlog management. Some backlog-management work can be delegated, but that does not transfer the accountability.

text.title: Product Owner and Team Collaboration
text.content: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and effective backlog management.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: The Product Owner may delegate backlog-management work but remains accountable for it. Developers are responsible for sizing the work and deciding how selected work is performed. Clarify backlog items collaboratively while respecting the Product Owner’s ordering accountability and the Developers’ delivery decisions.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
In this hypothetical collaboration, the BA drafts clearer item wording and brings stakeholder questions to the group. The Product Owner remains accountable for ordering. Developers size the work and decide how selected work will be performed. The BA’s useful contribution is clarification that helps these decisions, not taking them over.

If a stakeholder asks the BA to promise a size or dictate the implementation approach, distinguish the BA’s requirements contribution from Developers' responsibility. If the BA updates backlog detail under delegated work, distinguish doing that task from becoming accountable for product value and backlog management.

The practical mental model is collaboration with explicit boundaries. People can contribute to the same item while retaining different accountabilities and delivery decisions. Clear descriptions support collaboration, but they should not be presented as authority to impose order, size, or implementation on the people accountable for those decisions.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Delegating backlog-management work does not transfer the Product Owner’s accountability. Nor does preparing requirements make the BA responsible for sizing or deciding how selected work is performed. Collaborate on clarity while respecting ordering and delivery boundaries.

practice_anchor.objective: Resolve role ambiguity in the hypothetical instruction-access item by matching proposed actions to the appropriate role: BA clarification, Product Owner accountability for product value and backlog management including ordering, or Developers' responsibility for sizing and implementation decisions.
practice_anchor.success: The matches form a collaboration approach in which the BA drafts clearer wording and brings stakeholder questions, the Product Owner retains accountability even when backlog-management tasks are delegated, and Developers size the work and decide how selected work is performed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the collaboration boundaries visible around the instruction-access item: BA contributions clarify requirements, Product Owner accountability covers product value and backlog management including ordering, and Developers own sizing and decisions about how selected work is performed. Annotate delegated backlog work to show that accountability remains with the Product Owner.

notes: Do not conflate BA contribution with Product Owner or Developer authority.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for Developers focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal and an actionable plan.
Participation by other Scrum accountabilities as Developers depends on actively working on iteration backlog items.
Give an update that identifies an impediment or needed coordination affecting the goal and the next work plan.
Move detailed replanning discussion outside the Daily Scrum rather than extending the event.

text.content: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for Developers focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal and an actionable plan. Other Scrum accountabilities participate as Developers when actively working on iteration backlog items. For example: “The instruction clarification blocks this goal-related item; I need coordination to resolve it, then continue the planned work.” Keep detailed replanning outside the event rather than extending it.

practice_anchor.objective: Write a brief Daily Scrum update for the hypothetical situation in which an instruction clarification blocks a goal-related backlog item. Identify the impediment, needed coordination, and next work plan.
practice_anchor.success: The update connects the clarification blocker to the Sprint Goal, states the coordination needed to resolve it, and identifies the work to continue afterward. It leaves detailed replanning outside the 15-minute event rather than becoming a detailed status report.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show two updates for the same instruction-clarification scenario: a concise update annotated with goal impact, blocker, needed coordination, and next work plan; and a detailed status report annotated to identify discussion that belongs outside the Daily Scrum.

notes: Keep brief; no automatic BA attendance rule.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome with stakeholders and determines future adaptations; it is a working session rather than just a presentation.
Acceptance criteria provide the story-specific conditions used to judge whether delivered behavior satisfies the need.
Compare the demonstrated behavior with those conditions and discuss differences with the stakeholders.

text.content: Imagine stakeholders examining the iteration’s order-service outcome. The Sprint Review is a working session for inspecting that outcome and determining future adaptations, not merely a polished presentation.

text.title: Sprint Review (BA Involvement)
text.content: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome with stakeholders and determines future adaptations; it is a working session rather than just a presentation.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Acceptance criteria provide the story-specific conditions used to judge whether delivered behavior satisfies the need. Compare the demonstrated behavior with those conditions and discuss differences with the stakeholders.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical story, acceptance conditions say that selecting an existing order displays current instructions and an unknown identifier displays a not-found result. Compare the demonstrated behavior with those story-specific conditions. If the unknown-identifier case behaves differently, discuss that difference with stakeholders rather than relying on a general claim that the demo looked successful.

Use the inspection to discuss future adaptations. The conditions help judge whether the demonstrated behavior satisfies the particular need, while the review addresses the outcome with stakeholders. Keep the example’s conditions visible so participants can connect what they saw with what was expected.

The useful BA contribution is evidence-based comparison and discussion of differences. Use the inspection for collaborative adaptation rather than treating the event as a one-way show.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A presentation of features alone does not capture the review’s working-session purpose. Compare behavior with the story’s acceptance conditions and discuss differences with stakeholders. A convincing demonstration is not evidence that every specified condition was met.

practice_anchor.objective: Compare supplied demonstration observations for the hypothetical order-service feature with its acceptance criteria: an existing order displays current instructions, and an unknown identifier displays a not-found result. Select any mismatched observations and identify the corresponding unmet criterion.
practice_anchor.success: Correctly distinguish matching behavior from mismatches, associate each mismatch with its original acceptance criterion, and identify the difference to raise with stakeholders.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the hypothetical order-service acceptance criteria beside the corresponding demonstrated behavior, with mismatches clearly marked for stakeholder discussion.

media.group_title: Sprint Review: inspection, feedback, and adaptation

segments.label: Inspect the outcome and make room for stakeholder feedback
segments.summary: A Sprint Review brings participants, including real end users, together to inspect delivered work and adapt based on what they discover. The example concerns an improved table component for creating and editing broadcasting work orders. The narrator points out that the Product Owner is enthusiastic about showing completed work but has not left enough room for feedback. A demonstration is only the beginning of a review: it should trigger stakeholder feedback rather than end the discussion.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the work-order example distinguishes showing delivered work from inviting feedback. The clip uses “increment” for the delivered outcome that participants inspect together.
bridge_note.after: The clip establishes inspection and feedback, but does not explain acceptance criteria or compare behavior against them. The text supplies those story-specific conditions and explains how to discuss mismatches.

notes: Do not introduce Definition of Done rules before their concept; keep review focused on inspection and adaptation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: The Sprint Retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness.
Review what went well, what problems occurred, and how they were or were not solved, considering interactions, processes, and tools.
Identify a concrete change that would improve effectiveness and arrange to address the most helpful improvements promptly.

text.content: Suppose the team completed an iteration but spent significant effort clarifying instruction wording late in the work. The retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness; it is not another stakeholder presentation of the product outcome.

text.title: Sprint Retrospective (BA Involvement)
text.content: The Sprint Retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Review what went well, what problems occurred, and how they were or were not solved, considering interactions, processes, and tools. Identify a concrete change that would improve effectiveness and arrange to address the most helpful improvements promptly.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Review what went well, what problems occurred, and how those problems were or were not solved. In this hypothetical discussion, clear customer examples worked well, while late uncertainty about “current instructions” interrupted work. Consider interactions, processes, and tools rather than treating the issue as only one person’s performance.

Identify a concrete change. The team might agree to clarify instruction examples during refinement and arrange to address that helpful improvement promptly. That is an example action chosen for this situation, not a mandatory retrospective technique.

The useful output is a specific improvement the team intends to address, grounded in its review. A record saying only “communicate better” leaves the change unclear. Keep the discussion connected to what happened and what can improve effectiveness, including whether earlier problems were actually solved. The focus is learning about the team’s way of working, not inventing a new product requirement simply because the team has held a meeting.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A retrospective is not just a list of complaints or a repeat of the Sprint Review. It examines quality and effectiveness and leads toward concrete improvements. Naming a problem without identifying a helpful change does not complete that purpose.

practice_anchor.objective: Record one actionable retrospective improvement for the hypothetical sprint in which clear customer examples worked well but late uncertainty about current instructions interrupted work.
practice_anchor.success: The recorded item identifies a concrete change to the team's way of working, connects it to the described sprint events, explains how it could improve quality or effectiveness, and specifies how the team will arrange to address it promptly rather than merely stating a complaint.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the connection between the sprint's late instruction uncertainty and a concrete improvement: contrast the vague item 'communicate better' with clarifying instruction examples during refinement and arranging to address that change promptly.

notes: Avoid unsupported retrospective ceremonies or mandatory voting methods.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Five Whys traces a problem’s cause by repeatedly asking why the previous explanation occurred.
Write the problem, ask why it happened, record the answer, and ask why that answer happened to extend the causal chain.
Five is a guide rather than a required stopping point; use the chain to reach an underlying cause rather than restating the symptom.

text.content: Imagine the problem statement is “Dispatch preparation is delayed by clarification calls.” Ask why those calls occurred. In this hypothetical causal chain, staff could not find current instructions. Ask why that happened: amended instructions remained in a separate record. Ask why they remained separate: the handoff did not identify where the current instruction record should be updated.

text.title: Five Whys
text.content: Five Whys traces a problem’s cause by repeatedly asking why the previous explanation occurred.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Write the problem, ask why it happened, record the answer, and ask why that answer happened to extend the causal chain. Five is a guide rather than a required stopping point; use the chain to reach an underlying cause rather than restating the symptom.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Write each answer and use it as the starting point for the next why question. The chain moves from the stated problem toward an underlying cause instead of repeatedly renaming “dispatch delay.” These answers are assumptions provided for the exercise, not a factual diagnosis of a real team’s process.

Five is a guide, not a required stopping point. Do not invent a fifth explanation merely to reach the technique’s name, and do not stop automatically at five if the chain has not reached an underlying cause. Keep the successive explanation visible so a reader can follow how the cause of the previous explanation is being examined.

The useful output is a recorded causal chain tied to the original problem. The technique is not a guarantee that the first plausible answer is the true cause. Repeated why questions should extend the underlying explanation rather than restate the symptom.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: “Why?” followed by the same symptom in different words does not extend the causal chain. Five is not a compulsory count. Avoid manufacturing answers to fill five lines or treating the technique’s name as proof that the fifth answer must be the root cause.

practice_anchor.objective: Apply Five Whys to the hypothetical dispatch-preparation problem by arranging the supplied causal answers in sequence, recording the why connection between each pair, and stating the underlying cause. (Fact citations: f1, f2, f3.)
practice_anchor.success: The recorded chain proceeds from clarification calls to staff being unable to find current instructions, then to amended instructions remaining in a separate record, and finally to the handoff not identifying where the current instruction record should be updated. The learner states that final explanation as the exercise's underlying cause, distinguishes it from dispatch delay, and does not invent additional answers to reach five.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the hypothetical dispatch causal chain visible, with the original symptom, successive recorded explanations linked by why, and the underlying handoff cause clearly distinguished from the symptom. (Fact citations: f1, f2, f3.)

media.group_title: Five Whys: from symptom to underlying cause

segments.label: Five Whys: trace a machine stoppage to its underlying cause
segments.summary: Five Whys extends a causal chain by asking why each previous explanation occurred. The example traces a machine stoppage through a blown fuse, overload, insufficient bearing lubrication, a pump that fails to draw lubricant, and a worn pump shaft. The underlying cause identified is a missing strainer that allowed metal chips to damage the pump. Following the explanations back toward the stoppage helps check the chain's causal logic. The number of questions is flexible: three or eight may be appropriate if they reach an underlying cause rather than stop at a symptom.

bridge_note.before: Watch how each why builds on the previous explanation in the machine example. The clip also calls Five Whys a causal chain; focus on the connections, not the number of questions.
bridge_note.after: The clip distinguishes an underlying cause from a symptom and makes the question count flexible. It does not teach the written-answer workflow; the text explains how to record and extend the chain.

notes: All sample causal answers are hypothetical; do not present guesses as verified real causes.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes of a problem to support root cause analysis.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/fishbone-diagram — What is a fishbone diagram template?

required_facts.statement: Write a specific problem statement, select cause categories appropriate to the problem, and brainstorm potential causes with the team.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/fishbone-diagram — Define the problem; Choose categories; Brainstorm potential causes

required_facts.statement: Place each proposed cause under its category branch to expose patterns; then analyze the proposed causes and agree actions addressing the root cause.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/confluence/templates/fishbone-diagram — Organize causes; Analyze the diagram; Develop an action plan

text.content: Suppose the specific problem is “Orders wait for instruction clarification before dispatch.” A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes for analysis rather than declaring every proposed cause proven.

text.title: Fishbone Diagram
text.content: A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes of a problem to support root cause analysis.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Write a specific problem statement, select cause categories appropriate to the problem, and brainstorm potential causes with the team. Place each proposed cause under its category branch to expose patterns; then analyze the proposed causes and agree actions addressing the root cause.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical team discussion, select categories suited to the problem, such as information, handoffs, and tools. Write the problem statement and brainstorm potential causes. Place “amendments stored separately” under information, “unclear update responsibility” under handoffs, and “difficult instruction lookup” under tools. These category names and causes are example choices, not a mandatory universal set.

Use the branches to expose patterns in the proposed causes. Then analyze them and agree actions addressing the root cause. Do not jump from a busy branch to a causal conclusion without that analysis. The diagram’s organizational role helps the team see possibilities; the later analysis is what examines them.

The useful output is a structured cause discussion connected to a specific problem, followed by analyzed causes and agreed actions. A vague problem such as “everything is slow” gives the branches less focus than a concrete statement about waiting for clarification. Keep potential causes explicitly potential until they have been analyzed rather than labeling the diagram a proof of cause.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Putting a cause on a branch does not verify it. A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes, which still need analysis before actions address the root cause. The categories should suit the problem, not be treated as a fixed set every business must use.

practice_anchor.objective: Build a fishbone diagram for the problem “Orders wait for instruction clarification before dispatch.” Create at least three appropriate category branches and place the candidate causes “amendments stored separately,” “unclear update responsibility,” and “difficult instruction lookup” under suitable branches.
practice_anchor.success: The diagram displays the specific problem, at least three relevant category branches, and each candidate cause on an appropriate branch. For example, information, handoffs, and tools accommodate the three supplied causes respectively. Other suitable category choices are acceptable, and the causes remain labeled as possibilities rather than proven root causes.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible the specific dispatch-clarification problem connected to at least three labeled category branches, with proposed causes placed beneath their corresponding categories. Keep the organization of possible causes distinct from subsequent analysis and agreement on actions.

notes: Do not add mandatory cause-category lists or infer cause from number of suggestions.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: The Definition of Done describes the state of an increment when it meets the required quality measures.
The Scrum Team follows a shared Definition of Done, at least as rigorous as any organizational standard.
An item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review.
Check the completed work against the defined quality criteria and identify any unmet criterion before calling it done.
Story acceptance criteria specify completion conditions for that particular story rather than replacing the shared quality standard.

text.content: Imagine a team has a shared Definition of Done for an increment. In this hypothetical standard, required quality measures include passing the agreed checks and completing the agreed review. The exact checks are invented for the exercise; the shared standard must be at least as rigorous as any applicable organizational standard.

text.title: Definition of Done
text.content: The Definition of Done describes the state of an increment when it meets the required quality measures.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: The Scrum Team follows a shared Definition of Done, at least as rigorous as any organizational standard. An item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review. Check the completed work against the defined quality criteria and identify any unmet criterion before calling it done. Story acceptance criteria specify completion conditions for that particular story rather than replacing the shared quality standard.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Before calling work done, check it against every defined quality criterion and identify unmet criteria. If one required review remains incomplete, the item does not meet the Definition of Done. Under the stated Scrum rule, an item that does not meet it cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review.

Now compare that with a story’s acceptance condition, such as “Selecting an existing order displays current instructions.” The condition specifies completion for this particular story. Even if the behavior satisfies that condition, it does not replace the shared quality standard. The learner needs to distinguish story-specific behavior from the state required of the increment.

The useful output is a clear check against the shared standard, not a subjective declaration that the work looks finished. Keep unmet criteria visible and do not quietly lower the standard to match what was completed. The BA can help clarify story conditions while the Scrum Team follows the shared Definition of Done.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Passing a story’s acceptance criteria does not replace the shared Definition of Done. An item with an unmet required quality criterion cannot be labeled done, released, or presented at Sprint Review under the Definition of Done rule. Do not reinterpret that as merely optional reporting guidance.

A completed story acceptance condition is not treated as a substitute for the shared standard, and any unmet required criterion prevents the item from being marked done, released, or presented at Sprint Review.
